title: Dialysis access complications
subtitle: Bleeding, thrombosis and steal in AV fistulas and grafts

sources.title: Vascular Access: 2018 Clinical Practice Guidelines of the ESVS
KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Vascular Access: 2019 Update

red_flags.text: Active bleeding from a fistula or graft. High-flow access can exsanguinate a patient in minutes, including at home overnight.
Thin, shiny or ulcerated skin over an aneurysmal fistula, a scab that keeps recurring, or a small bleed: warning signs of imminent rupture.
A cold, painful, weak or numb hand on the access side, especially rest pain, tissue loss or a motor deficit: severe access-related hand ischaemia (steal).
Pain, weakness and numbness in the hand immediately after access creation with a warm hand and a radial pulse: ischaemic monomelic neuropathy.
Loss of thrill and bruit, or a missed dialysis session. Check the potassium before anything else.
Erythema, pus or exposed graft over a prosthetic access: graft infection with risk of anastomotic blow-out.

do_now.text: Bleeding access: firm digital pressure exactly on the bleeding point, arm elevated, without occluding the whole access for long. A tourniquet proximal to the bleed for life-threatening haemorrhage that pressure does not control.
Skin breakdown or bleeding over an access aneurysm: urgent surgical review and do not cannulate that segment.
Thrombosed access: check potassium and fluid status first, dialyse through a temporary catheter if needed, and refer for declotting promptly to avoid losing the access.
Suspected ischaemic monomelic neuropathy: immediate vascular surgical review. Urgent ligation of the access is usually needed to save nerve function.

assess.text: Look, feel, listen: aneurysm, skin, thrill along the length, pulsatility (a hyperpulsatile access suggests outflow stenosis), and bruit.
Arm elevation test: a fistula that does not collapse on elevation has an outflow stenosis.
Hand: colour, temperature, capillary refill, radial pulse with and without access compression, sensation and grip.
Grade hand ischaemia by severity: mild coldness and numbness only during dialysis differs from rest pain, tissue loss or motor deficit.
Dialysis history: recent flow problems, prolonged bleeding after needle removal, rising venous pressures.

investigate.text: Potassium, FBC and coagulation before any procedure on a thrombosed access or a patient who has missed dialysis.
Duplex ultrasound for stenosis, thrombus extent, aneurysm wall and access flow volume.
Fistulography or central venography for suspected central venous stenosis (arm swelling, collateral veins).
Digital pressures and access flow measurement to plan treatment for steal.

resuscitate.text: Major haemorrhage protocol for a shocked patient with an access bleed; reverse anticoagulation per local protocol.
Treat hyperkalaemia before taking a patient with a thrombosed access to theatre.
Never take blood pressure, place cannulae or apply a tourniquet routinely on the access arm.

definitive.text: Thrombosis: surgical thrombectomy or endovascular thrombectomy, always with treatment of the underlying stenosis, or the access will thrombose again.
Aneurysm with skin threat: surgical revision, resection with interposition, or ligation, as an urgent procedure.

Severe steal: flow reduction (banding) for high-flow access, or distal revascularisation with interval ligation, revision using distal inflow, or proximalisation of the arterial inflow. Ligation sacrifices the access and is the last option.
Infected prosthetic graft: excision of the infected graft, usually total, with antibiotics per local protocol.

escalate.text: Vascular access surgeon and interventional radiology together; renal team for dialysis planning.
Patients and carers should know how to apply pressure to a bleeding access and to call emergency services. Check that they do.
Transfer to the access centre for complex revision; do not let an unfamiliar team ligate a salvageable access.

notes: A fistula is a lifeline. Every decision should ask how to save it, unless saving it threatens the hand or the patient.
Fistula haemorrhage deaths are preventable: they are preceded by skin warning signs that someone saw.
Fix the stenosis, not just the clot. A declot without treating the cause buys days, not months.
